The figures follow a 3-step repeating cycle in the arrangement of the small black and white outer squares.

1st, 4th, 7th figures match
2nd, 5th, 8th figures match
so the 3rd, 6th, 9th figures must also match

Since the 3rd figure has the same pattern as B, the missing figure is B.

In each row, the third figure is a reduced version made from selected parts of the first two figures.
For the last row, the missing figure must keep only the outlined shapes needed to match the pattern: the small outlined square, the large outlined square, and the small horizontal rectangle.

Only C has that exact combination.

Group 1 contains only circles, and Group 2 contains only squares.

A and B fit Group 2 because they use squares only.
C fits Group 1 because it uses circles only.
D has both a square and a circle, so it does not follow either group rule.
Therefore, D belongs to neither group.

The figures work in pairs: in each pair, the top and bottom dot patterns swap places.

1st and 2nd figures are a pair
4th and 5th figures are a pair
so 6th and 7th figures must also be a pair

The 6th figure has 3 dots on top and 4 dots below, so the missing figure must have 4 dots on top and 3 dots below.

Therefore, D is the correct answer.

In Group 1, every figure contains a black diamond.
In Group 2, none of the figures contains a black diamond.

A and D fit Group 1 because they include a black diamond.
C fits Group 2 because it has no black diamond.
B has no black diamond, but it also does not match the pattern of Group 2 clearly.

Therefore, B belongs to neither group.

The top halves increase by pairs: 0, 0, 2, 2, 4, 4, so the next top half should be 6 dots.

The bottom halves also repeat in pairs: 3, 1, 3, 3, 3, 5, and after the change in the 6th figure, the missing one keeps the 3-dot diagonal pattern.

Therefore, A is the figure that completes the series.

The pattern builds a 3×3 grid step by step, adding one square at a time while keeping the alternating black–white arrangement consistent.

The next figure must complete the grid with the correct checkerboard pattern and proper placement of black and white squares.
 Only B correctly completes this pattern, so it is the answer.

The diamond moves around the corners in order: bottom-left → top-left → top-right → bottom-right, so the next position returns to bottom-left.

At the same time, the line changes orientation in a cycle: vertical → diagonal → horizontal → diagonal → vertical.

Therefore, the next figure must have the diamond at the bottom-left and a vertical line, which is C.

The pattern alternates between a simple split figure and a more divided figure.

1st figure: simple horizontal split
2nd figure: more divided vertical version
3rd figure: more divided horizontal version
4th figure: more divided vertical version

So the next figure should return to a simple horizontal split, but with the colors reversed from the 1st figure.

Therefore, C is the correct answer.

The pattern is moving toward more starred squares from one figure to the next.

In the 4th figure, the starred squares already occupy most of the middle pattern, so the next figure should place them in the remaining matching positions while keeping the center black, the top-middle and bottom-middle white, and the bottom-left black.

Only A fits that completed arrangement.

The black region keeps increasing from one figure to the next, while the slanting edge shifts position around the square.

The missing figure should therefore have more black area than the 4th figure and keep the same angled boundary pattern.

Only D matches this continued growth and placement of the sloping white section.

From the first pair, the figure is changed by turning the horizontal double bars into vertical double bars, while the other symbols keep their relative positions after the rearrangement.

Applying the same change to the lower-left figure places the small outlined square at the top-left and the black square with white center at the bottom-right, with the double vertical bars in the middle.

Therefore, D is the correct answer.

From the first pair, the pattern is changed by moving the top-left black square to the top-right, while the other squares shift to keep the same overall arrangement.

Applying the same change to the lower-left figure gives a pattern with white squares at the two top corners, black squares at the bottom corners, and white squares in the center column.

Therefore, B is the correct answer.

From the first pair, the black area moves to the opposite larger region, while the small outlined square changes to the opposite side and the dividing lines keep the same structure.

Applying that same change to the lower-left figure gives a figure with the top half black and the small outlined square at the bottom-right.

Therefore, B is the correct answer.

From the first pair, the two corner squares swap their inner shading, and the middle line pattern changes from horizontal to vertical while keeping the same diagonal connection.

Applying the same change to the lower-left figure gives a figure with the vertical middle line, the hook on the upper-left side, and the corner squares switched in the same way.

Therefore, C is the correct answer.

In the first pair, the small outer squares are moved into the center to form a 2×2 block, while keeping their black/white arrangement.

Applying the same rule to the lower-left figure, the four diagonal outer squares must also move into the center with the same positions preserved.

Only D gives that correct central black-and-white arrangement.

The missing part must match both the outer frame pattern and the inner small-square pattern.

In that corner of the grid, the two top cells are plain empty squares.
The lower cell must contain the small white square with the diagonal corner lines in the correct orientation.
 Only C fits both the blank top cells and the correct lower-left inner pattern.

The figures follow a repeating order of shape types around the grid: square-in-square, diamond, square, circle, then the same pattern continues with the filled/outline style changing by position.

The missing L-shaped part must therefore contain a filled circle, a square-in-square, and an outline square in the correct order.
 Only B matches that pattern.

All the other figures (A, C, D, E) follow a consistent rule: the white shape is formed by combining or extending triangular parts along a diagonal direction.

Figure B is different because its white shape is symmetrical and centered, forming a complete triangle without following the same directional “build” or extension pattern seen in the others.

In A, B, C, and E, the small square is placed on the opposite diagonal side of the two large corner squares, creating a shifting diagonal relationship.

D is different because the small square is positioned so that the arrangement does not match the same diagonal pattern followed by the others.

In B, C, D, and E, the short vertical rectangle is placed in a different position from the large square, so the two shapes are separated clearly.

In A, the short vertical rectangle and the large square are arranged in a way that breaks this common placement pattern.

In A, B, C, and D, the extra small divided section is placed in a way that keeps the inner lines connected to the same general corner-based pattern.

E is different because the small divided part is positioned on the right side, breaking the placement pattern followed by the other four figures.
The answer here is “S” because it is the only letter with curves.

In A, B, C, and E, the two shapes are of the same type or are both simple outline figures without one clearly containing the other.

D is different because it combines two different shape types — a square and a triangle — in a distinct overlapping arrangement.

Therefore, D is the odd one out.

The correct answer is B because it is the only one that is not used as a means of
communication or is not powered by electricity.

The correct answer is C. The circle in each shape is divided according to the
shape’s number of sides. The pentagon is the only shape that has a circle divided
not similar to the number of sides.

In A, C, D, and E, there is at least one repeated pair of identical figures placed together (such as two squares, two diamonds, or two small diagonal squares).

B is different because, although it has a pair of black diamonds and a pair of small squares, its overall set includes a single black diamond that breaks the pair-based grouping pattern followed more neatly by the others.

In A, B, D, and E, the figures follow a balanced pattern of alternating white and black top squares across the row.

In C, this pattern is broken because there are two black top squares placed consecutively at the beginning.
3 is the only choice facing a different direction and has a different  design.
choice 3 is the only one facing the different direction when rotated.

choices 1 & 2 matches 3 & 4 when rotated counterclockwise. Only
choice 5 does not have a matching pair.
the other choices are more curved cut compared to figure 4
all figures are the same, just rotated, except 4.
the point of figure 4 is facing a different direction

in choice 1, the shorter lines on the longer line are nearer compared to
the others
choice 7 is the only face with a straight flat-nose
the lines pass through the semicircle except for figure 4
all cuts are on the left side of the figure when facing upward except 5

The pattern adds one new square at each step, building from left to right around the border, while the black–white colors keep alternating in each vertical column.

The next figure should therefore add the right column and keep the same alternating arrangement, giving black–white–black on both sides with a white square in the bottom center.

Therefore, A best completes the series.

The pattern alternates between an empty center and a filled center: empty, filled, empty, filled, so the next one must be empty again.

Also, the vertical line becomes longer in pairs: short, short, long, long, so the next figure keeps the long vertical line.
Therefore, C best completes the series.

The main shape changes in a cycle: diamond → square + diamond → square → square outline, then the pattern starts again with a diamond.

At the same time, the short line also cycles through positions/orientations, and the next figure should return to the vertical line arrangement.

Therefore, C best completes the series.

The figures alternate between filled central shapes and small corner marks:

1st: large filled shapes
2nd: small corner squares
3rd: large filled shapes
4th: small corner squares

So the 5th should again be a figure with large filled shapes in the center.

Also, the central filled shapes change form from rectangles to diamonds, so the next matching step is the triangle form.
Therefore, D best completes the series.

In the first pair, the side parts are compressed into the center, so the outer shapes disappear and only the central part remains inside the box.

Applying the same rule to the lower figure, the two black side blocks combine into a single central black rectangle.

Therefore, C best completes the series.

From the first pair, both small squares move one step clockwise inside the large shape.

Applying the same rule to the hexagon:

the black square moves from top-left to middle-left
the white square moves from bottom-right to bottom-left

Therefore, A best completes the series.

In each row and column, the middle figure is the combination of the two outer figures.

Row 1: left + right = middle
Row 2: left + right = middle
So Row 3 must follow the same rule

In the last row, the left figure has the vertical oval with a black square, and the middle figure adds the horizontal oval plus the small white square at the top-left.
So the missing right figure must supply only the horizontal oval and the small white square.

Therefore, A best completes the series.

In A, B, D, and E, the two end squares are placed on opposite sides of the horizontal line — one above and one below.

In C, both end squares do not follow that opposite-side arrangement in the same way, so it breaks the pattern.
Therefore, C does not belong to the series.

In B, C, D, and E, the two black squares stay adjacent in the rotation pattern, and the whole figure can be seen as a turned version of the same arrangement.

A is different because its black and white squares do not match that same rotational arrangement.

Therefore, A does not belong to the series.

Group 1 contains figures made from straight-edged shapes only, while Group 2 contains figures made from curved shapes only.

A and B fit Group 1 because their shapes are straight-edged.
D fits Group 2 because its set follows the curved-shape group pattern.
C mixes curved shapes with a straight-edged diamond, so it does not fit either group.

Therefore, C belongs in neither group.

The number inside each shape follows the rule:

number = (number of sides × 2) − 6

Triangle: 3 × 2 − 6 = 0
Square: 4 × 2 − 6 = 2
Pentagon: 5 × 2 − 6 = 4 — but the figure shows 5, so the pattern is more simply increasing with the shape progression toward the hexagon choice set.

A cleaner way to see it is that the shape gains one side each step, and the number also increases to match the next required value for the hexagon.
The best completing figure is the hexagon with 9, so C.

The arrow moves one side around the pentagon each step and also reverses direction: right, down, left, so the next should be on the next side and point accordingly.

At the same time, the 4 dots become 3 dots, matching the pattern shown before.

Therefore, B best completes the series.

The numbers follow the pattern 17, 9, 5, ? — each time, the value is reduced by about half:

17 → 9
9 → 5
so 5 → 3

Also, the dots decrease step by step, matching the choice with 3.

Therefore, C best completes the series.

The inner shape loses one side each step:

1st: square (4 sides)
2nd: 3-sided open shape
3rd: 2-sided angle
so the 4th should have 1 side only

At the same time, the diagonal corner line keeps moving to the next corner position.

Therefore, B best completes the series.

The same three shapes are being rearranged in order: triangle, square/diamond, and circle.
Each figure changes which shape is outer, middle, and inner.

1st: triangle outside, square middle, circle inside
2nd: square outside, circle middle, diamond inside
3rd: circle outside, diamond middle, triangle inside

So the next figure should continue the cycle with the diamond outside, triangle in the middle, and circle inside.

Therefore, B best completes the series.

Each figure adds one new symbol and the symbols keep moving clockwise around the spokes.

Also, the pattern keeps the same balance of filled and unfilled shapes as it grows:

1st: 2 circles
2nd: adds 1 square
3rd: adds another square
4th: adds 1 triangle
so the next figure must place the symbols in the next rotated positions.

Only D matches that next arrangement, so it best completes the series.

The pattern changes the filled region step by step: first the circle is filled, then the rectangle, then the triangle. The next step is for the outer background/square area to become filled.

At the same time, the circle changes to keep the opposite color of the newly filled main region.

Therefore, A best completes the series.

Short explanation:
The pattern is simplifying the figure step by step.

1st figure: outer shape + inner triangle
2nd figure: only the triangle remains
3rd figure should be the inverted version of that triangle
4th figure then changes into the crossed-square pattern

Therefore, A best completes the series.

Short explanation:
The top number increases by 60 each step:

60, 120, 180, 240

The bottom number is the top number divided by twice the number of sides of the shape:

Triangle: 60 ÷ 6 = 10
Square: 120 ÷ 8 = 15
Pentagon: 180 ÷ 10 = 18
Hexagon: 240 ÷ 12 = 20

So the missing figure should be 240 over 20, which is B.

The black block moves clockwise around the edges: bottom → left → top → right → bottom.

At the same time, the inner shapes (rectangle and semicircle) shift positions consistently with this rotation.

The next position should return the black block to the bottom side, which matches D.

The full/half vertical black bar repeats every 2 diagrams, the middle figure and its pattern repeats every 3
diagrams.
Count the number of figures; it should follow a diagram with 2 figurines. Color doesn`t matter.
A 5 lines/dots figurine should follow. Count the number of sides or dots and you can see that every 2 figurines the number of lines/dots increases with 1. Color doesn`t matter.
A figure with 12 dots should follow because at each step an increasing increment (1, 2, 3, 4) is added to the number of dots of the previous figurine.

The heart moves anti-clock-wise from corner to corner. The triangle moves clock-wise, to the opposite corner of the same square side and it rotes 90 degrees on itself so that it’s aligned with the next square side that follows.

Consider that columns are A, B, C, D and lines are numbered from 1 to 4. The logic is: the black cell situated at A1 moves horizontally 1 cell to the right, the B2 black cell moves diagonally from top right to bottom left, and the D3 black cell moves vertically 1 cell up.
The black boxes cells are (mirror) reflected on the vertical axis.

Each 3 rd diagram results from over-lapping the first 2 diagrams. Position doesn’t change, but if a black and white figurine overlap they neutralize each other and don’t show anymore in the composed diagram.
The arrows at the bottom show how the figurines on the same column are moving. A black arrow also reverts the colors of the figurines; a white arrow has no effect on the color.

The black figurines move horizontally one position to the left only for the odd number diagrams, the white figurines move always one position horizontally to the right, and the dotted star shows always to the left of the black triangle.

The pattern alternates between horizontal and vertical arrangements:

1st: simple horizontal split
2nd: simple vertical split
3rd: divided horizontal version
4th: divided vertical version

So the next figure should return to a simple horizontal split, but with the colors reversed from the first figure.

Therefore, C best completes the series.

The pattern alternates in two ways:

the long vertical line goes full, lower half, full, lower half, so the next one should be full again
the short horizontal arm switches side: left, right, left, right, so the next should be on the left

Therefore, D best completes the series.

The pattern is building the outer frame step by step while keeping the colors in an alternating order.

1st figure: only the left column
2nd figure: adds the top row
3rd figure: adds the bottom row
4th figure: adds more of the inside/right side pattern

So the next figure should complete the missing right column and keep the same black–white arrangement.

Therefore, A best completes the series.

Each figure contains three black shapes and one white shape. The types of shapes also change in a pattern from one box to the next.

The missing figure should continue that pattern with two black triangles, one white rectangle, and no extra unmatched shape.

Therefore, A best completes the series.

The pattern removes one outer layer at each step:

1st: three nested squares with a vertical divider
2nd: two layers with a horizontal divider
3rd: one layer with a vertical divider
4th: one layer with a horizontal divider

So the next figure should be the simplest remaining form with the divider switching back to vertical.

Therefore, B best completes the series.

From the first pair, the figure is changed by reversing it left-to-right: the corner squares switch sides, the diagonal line slants the opposite way, and the horizontal/vertical line keeps its matching position.

Applying the same change to the lower-left figure gives the version with the top-left and bottom-right squares swapped in mirror position and the diagonal line reversed.

Therefore, B is the correct answer.

From the first pair, the white squares shift to the right side while the remaining positions become black, preserving the overall arrangement pattern.

Applying the same change to the lower-left figure gives a result with:

top row: black, black, white
middle row: white, black, black
bottom row: black, black, white

Therefore, D best completes the series.

From the first pair, the whole figure is transformed by a 180° rotation: the black square moves from the top-left to the top-right area, and the smaller internal line details shift accordingly.

Applying the same rule to the lower-left figure places the black square at the lower-left, with the short line moved to the upper-right and the other parts rotated into place.

Therefore, A is the correct answer.

From the first pair, the figure changes by moving the two middle white squares into the bottom corners, while the center area becomes black.

Applying the same rule to the lower-left figure gives a result with:

white squares in the top-left and both bottom corners
black squares in the top-right and middle-left/middle-center

Therefore, C best completes the series.

From the first pair, the figure changes by removing the outer circle and simplifying the spokes, while keeping the same relative positions of the black and white small squares.

Applying the same rule to the lower-left figure gives a pattern where the left and right horizontal black squares stay, the top-right and bottom-left white squares stay, and the circle is removed.

Therefore, D completes the statement.

In B, C, D, and E, the two corner squares swap their inner types consistently with the direction of the bent line and diagonal connection.

A is different because its corner-square arrangement does not match the same transformation pattern followed by the other four.

Therefore, A is the odd one out.

In A, C, D, and E, the figure contains one angular shape plus one or two circles, with the main shapes overlapping in a more mixed arrangement.

B is different because it is the only one made of a square with two circles only, without the same mixed shape pattern seen in the others.

Therefore, B is the odd one out.

In A, B, C, and D, the black squares shift around the cross in a consistent rotation pattern.

E breaks that pattern because its black-and-white arrangement does not match the same rotational order followed by the other four.

Therefore, E is the odd one out.

In A, B, D, and E, the right column contains both a black and a white square, so the colors are mixed on that side.

C is different because its right column is all black, which breaks the pattern followed by the others.

Therefore, C is the odd one out.

In A, B, C, and E, the top small square is white and the two black squares stay on the horizontal left–right arms.

D is different because one black square is moved to the upper-left diagonal arm, so it breaks the common arrangement.

Therefore, D is the odd one out.

Short explanation:
The figures follow two patterns:

the long line alternates by row: horizontal, vertical, horizontal
the small black rectangle moves upward/rightward through the set

In the last position, the missing figure must return to a horizontal long line and place the other small shapes in the matching top and bottom positions.

Only B fits that arrangement.

In each row, the third figure shows only the positions that stay the same in the first two figures. The changing extra small squares are removed.

Applying that to the last row, the common remaining positions are the left white square, the bottom white square, and the lower-right white square, with the same main spokes kept.

Therefore, A best completes the series.

Group 1 uses circles, and Group 2 uses squares/rectangles.

A and B fit Group 2 because they contain only square-based shapes.
D fits Group 1 because it contains circles only.
C does not fit either group because, although it has circles, its arrangement does not follow the same grouping rule as Group 1.

Therefore, C belongs in neither group.

In both Group 1 and Group 2, the figures normally have arrows arranged with a balanced opposite-direction pattern around the center.

A is different because its arrows do not follow that same balance—the arrangement is uneven compared with the figures in both groups.

Therefore, A belongs in neither group.

The figures follow a repeating 3-step cycle:

top empty, bottom 4
top 1, bottom 6
top 4, bottom 1

Then it repeats in changed form:
4. top 1, bottom 6
5. top empty, bottom 3
6. top 1, bottom 6

So the next figure should match the next step in the cycle, with 2 dots on top and 1 dot below.

Therefore, D is the best next figure.

The top half alternates: 4, 1, 4, 1, 4, 0, so the next returns to 4 dots.

The bottom half decreases step by step in this part of the series: 6, 0, 5, 1, 3, 1, so the next should be 2 dots.

Therefore, B best completes the series.

The grid is built from matching corner sections. The missing L-shaped piece must continue all three local patterns:

top-left cell: vertical split
top-right cell: horizontal bands with the small inner rectangle
bottom-left cell: diagonal corner line

Only C matches all three surrounding patterns, so it completes the grid.

The missing L-shaped piece must continue the three surrounding patterns:

the diagonal small-square corner at the left of the piece
the vertical double-line strip at the lower part
the black filled corner-squares in the upper-right part

Only D matches all of these connections, so it completes the grid.

In A, B, D, and E, the five circles follow a consistent progression in the positions of the small black squares from left to right.

Row C breaks that pattern because one of its figures does not fit the same step-by-step arrangement followed by the others.

Therefore, C is the odd one out.

In A, B, C, and D, the six symbols are the same set arranged in a shifted order. They can be seen as rotations of one common sequence.

E breaks that order because its symbols are not in the same cyclic arrangement as the other four.

Therefore, E is the odd one out.

In the abstract reasoning sequence displayed above, two distinct patterns can be observed:
Placing a square or rhomb alternating within or outside the circle.
Each additional figure changes the location of the square / rhomb by a quarter turn
counterclockwise rotation.
This results in the alternately placing of a rhomb and square, respectively, within and outside the
circle, keeping in mind that the change of position follows the quarter turn counterclockwise
rotation. The solution to this abstract reasoning sequence is therefore the 4th one, where the
square is positioned at the bottom and outside the circle.

In this test the degree of symmetry of the figure placed within the circle decreases step by step. The pattern starts with a circle, a line, a triangle and so on, continuing with lower symmetry
objects (and thus more side faces). This automatically results in a hexagon placed in the circle as
the solution for this abstract reasoning sequence.

The sequence clearly shows that the position of the star around the cross is the key to
solving this sequence. As the sequence continues the location of the star is determined by a
quarter turn counterclockwise rotation every next figure. This results in the 4th solution where
the star is positioned at the bottom right part of the cross.

In the abstract reasoning sequence displayed, three distinct patterns can be observed:
The uppermost white circles with white crosses increase at first in number, after which the
amount of circles decrease in number again with increasing sequence.
The inner black circles with white crosses increase in number with increasing sequence.
The undermost white circles with black crosses decrease in number with increasing sequence.
Therefore the solution to this abstract reasoning sequence will consist of 1 uppermost circle, 5
middle ones and none at the bottom.

In the abstract reasoning sequence displayed, two distinct patterns can be observed:
As a basis the pattern consists at first of a circle, the highest form of symmetry. This degree of
symmetry decreases as the sequence increases which results in objects with more side faces.
Within these objects an arrow is present, which will be rotated counterclockwise by a quarter
turn with every next figure in the sequence.
This results in a hexagon with the inner arrow directed downwards.

Knowing the pattern of the position of the rhomb in the sequence is the key to solving
this sequence. The rhomb is rotated 450 counterclockwise in every following figure, at which the
colors within the rhomb alternate with each rotation. The solution to this sequence therefore is a
horizontal rhomb with the white side to the left.

The sequence should be seen as a series of stacked squares with alternating colors. At
every next figure in the sequence the uppermost square is removed, to end up with a black
square.

In this sequence two distinct patterns can be observed.
The persons face is alternately displayed from aside by increasing sequence.
The amount of black circles increases with increasing sequence.
This results in a person looking to the right with 5 black circles in the figure.

A rectangle is formed in parts in the abstract reasoning sequence. When modeling the
next rectangle, the first line of this second rectangle will be placed on top of the first line of the
first rectangle. This means that in a 3d view you would see depth in this figure. Since this is a 2d
view of the rectangle, it seems after modeling the first rectangle nothing is changed anymore.
The correct answer for this 2d view is therefore the first one, which only shows a rectangle.

A decrease in the amount of central squares with increasing sequence is the pattern in the
sequence displayed. However, this decrease is not steady; the first decrease consists of 1
central square, the second of 2 and the third again of 1, so the pattern is repeating itself with a
decrease in the amount of central squares. The solution to this abstract reasoning sequence will
thus be a blank space.

The number of circles decreases with increasing sequence in the picture displayed. This
decrease starts right at the top, moves to the left top and then continues at the right and left
bottom respectively. This pattern is repeated over and over again until no circles are left. That
means that the correct answer in this case the third image is.

The object in the figure above is rotated counterclockwise with increasing sequence, to create
new images as the sequence continues. The solution is therefore a vertical object, with in this
case the black side to the left as a result of the rotation.

In the abstract reasoning sequence displayed, three distinct patterns can be observed:
The image consists of a basic object containing a secondary object. These objects are color
incompatible and exchange color every next image in the sequence.
As the sequence progresses the degree of symmetry of the basic object decreases (a circle has
the highest degree of symmetry). This pattern of symmetry is repeated.
Next to that there is a difference when the pattern is repeated. The first pattern consists of the
same basic as secondary object. The second pattern however, consists of the secondary object of
its right neighbor image. This means that the solution consists of a black triangle as basic object
and a white circle as secondary object. This is the third solution.

The sequence starts with a circle containing a defined pattern. Next, a second circle with its own
pattern is placed at the right of the first circle. Subsequent a third circle with again a defined
pattern is placed to the left, next to the already existing circles. In this way the amount of defined
circles increases as the sequence increases, keeping in mind that the new circles are placed
alternately to the right and left respectively. This results in the second solution.

In the abstract reasoning sequence displayed above, two distinct patterns can be observed:
In every following figure in the sequence a smiley will be obtaining a hat.
The difficulty in this sequence is the change in position of the smiley with increasing sequence.
The smiley obtaining the hat will keep its position. The one on the right and across the one
receiving the hat however, will rotate 1800. Be aware of the fact that only the smiley rotates and
not the hat. When a smiley with a hat needs rotation, only the smiley rotates, resulting in a
smiley with a beard.
The solution to the sequence therefore consists of all smileys wearing hats / beards. The fourth
figure of the sequence shows that only the uppermost and the right smiley should be rotated.
This results in the fourth solution.

In the abstract reasoning sequence displayed, two distinct patterns can be observed:
As basic objects you have squares containing circles and vice versa present in the figure.
Next to that curls show up with increasing sequence, starting at the top and placed clockwise.
This results in a square containing a circle and 4 curls.

The abstract reasoning sequence consists of white and black circles. The sequence starts
with one black circle and continues with circles consisting of two and four parts respectively.
Next the amount of circle parts in decreased again to end up with one monochrome circle. In
this case a white circle, which is in agreement with the third solution.

In this sequence the time displayed on the clockworks is of importance to solving the row. The
uppermost left clockwork displays a time of 9.00h, the second 9.45h, the third 11.15h and the
last one 14.15h. A closer look at these times reveals that the difference between the first two
clockworks 45 minutes is, between the second and third 90 minutes and between the last two
180 minutes. Repeating this pattern, results in a difference between the fourth and fifth
clockwork of 360 minutes. The time displayed on the clockwork should thus be 20.15, which is
the second solution on the left.

In this abstract reasoning sequence the amount of leaflets is decreased as the sequence is
increased. First the uppermost left leaflet will fall off, then the undermost left leaflet. Next the
uppermost right leaflet will disappear, after which the logical next step will be the removal of the
undermost right leaflet and thus resulting in the third answer.

In order to obtain the answer from the sequence displayed above, the objects displayed in the
first figure of the sequence should switch places with each other:
First the two most right objects switch places with each other, resulting in the second figure.
Next, the circle and square will change places, resulting in the third figure. This means that

In the abstract reasoning sequence displayed above, three distinct patterns can be observed:
In every next figure in the sequence a vertical line will be added
Next to that also a diagonal line (uppermost left to undermost right) will be added at both sides
in every following figure. Since the first figure does not contain such a diagonal, the second
figure will contain 1 diagonal. In the following figures a diagonal at both sides of this starting
one will be placed.
The last pattern in this sequence contains the removal of diagonals (uppermost right to
undermost left). This removal will start in the centre and work its way up via the left diagonal to
the removal of the right one.
All these patterns combined result in the third answer. After all, this answer should contain 6
vertical stripes, 7 diagonals (uppermost left to undermost right) and 3 diagonals (uppermost
right to undermost left).
